persona.title: Pretend you are…
persona.text: Pretend you are Brian, 58, a trustee at a church in Illinois. Walt, the custodian, has looked after the church building for thirty years, and next month he retires. Only he knows where the water shutoff is, where the property deed is kept and which electrician understands the old wiring. Today you sit with him and put it all on one page, so the next custodian does not start from zero.

challenge.intro: Now you are Brian, sitting with Walt before he retires. The app is empty. Nobody will tell you which button to press. Use what you learned. Everything here is made up, so never type a real password. When you finish, tap Check my work.
challenge.start: Open The Key · Church Edition with the normal link (not the 🧪 test copy). If the welcome tour shows, tap 'skip the tour' → '✨ Start fresh with my own' → OK. Then scroll to the very bottom of the page and tap '🧹 Start fresh — erase this app’s data' → OK → OK (if it says 'There is nothing saved in this app yet', just tap OK). If a dark box says 'There are earlier notes saved here', tap 'Start fresh here'. All five sections are now empty.

tasks.text: The main water shutoff for the church is behind the kitchen, under a green metal cover. Put it where the next custodian will look for it.
tasks.hint: Taps, switches, keys and the alarm belong in the first section, 🏢 The building.

tasks.text: The church bank account is at First National Bank. The treasurer, Mrs. Hansen, and the pastor are on the account. The password list is in a sealed envelope in the office safe. The treasurer says 'just write the password, Grace2026'. Put the bank on the Key, the SAFE way.
tasks.hint: Bank accounts go in 💻 Accounts & services. Write who is on the account and where the password list is kept, never the password. If you typed Grace2026 anywhere, take it out.

tasks.text: The property deed for the church land is with the church lawyer in town, and a copy is in the office safe.
tasks.hint: Land papers go in 📄 Papers & policies. Say what the paper is and where it is kept.

tasks.text: If the lights fail, call the electrician John Miller at 847-555-0122. He knows the old wiring.
tasks.hint: People to call go in 🤝 The people to call. Write his name AND his phone number.

tasks.text: Walt has one last instruction: the sound system must be switched off after every Sunday service. Add it.
tasks.hint: Instructions that fit nowhere else go in the last section, 💌 Anything else they should know.

ownWords.question: In your own words, what is this app for?

so the knowledge is not only in one person's head when they leave

lines: This short video explains The Key, church edition. In about four minutes you will know what it is for and how to use it.

First, the problem. In many churches, one faithful person knows everything about the building. Where the water shutoff is. Who has keys. Which electrician knows the old wiring. Where the deed is kept.
Then that person retires or moves away. A pipe bursts on a Sunday morning, and nobody knows where to turn off the water.
The Key gets all of that out of one person's head and onto one printed page. You fill it in once, print it, and keep it in the church office.
Who uses it? A pastor, a trustee, a treasurer, a church secretary, or the volunteer who looks after the building.
One important rule. Never write a real password on this page. Only write where the password list is kept, for example, in a sealed envelope in the office safe.
Now the screen. At the top is the name of the app and what it is for. Under it, a bar shows how many of the five sections you have started.
Below that are the five sections. Tap a title to open it, and tap it again to fold it away. Each section has one writing box.
Tap the box and type, one thing per line. The grey example words show the kind of thing to write. They disappear when you start typing.
There is no Save button. Every letter saves on the phone as you type, so you can stop any time and come back later.
Section one is The building. The water shutoff, the breaker panels, the alarm, and where the keys are kept.
Section two is Accounts and services. The bank, the giving platform, the website, the utilities. Write who is on each account, and where the password list is kept.
Section three is Papers and policies. The deed, the insurance, the van title, the bylaws, contracts. Write which drawer, safe or lawyer has each one.
Section four is The people to call. The plumber, the electrician, the insurance agent, the member who fixes things. A name and a phone number for each.
Section five is Anything else they should know. A wish, an instruction, or a thank you, in your own words.
Under the sections is a safety reminder: never the passwords, only where they are kept.
Then the big button, Print my Key. It turns your five sections into one clean page with today's date. Print two copies: one for the office, one for the person you trust most.
Near the bottom, Start over empties all five boxes, after asking you first.
Under that, Save a copy keeps a backup file of your Key, and Bring a copy back restores it, on a new phone for example.
How to start? Pick the section you know best and write three lines. That is your first two minutes. The bar at the top fills as you go, and the rest can wait for another evening.
When you change something, like a new plumber or a new alarm company, open the app, fix the line, and print it again.
Privacy: everything stays only on this phone. There is no account, and nothing is sent to anyone.
The Key, church edition is nineteen dollars, once. Profits help students in Kenya stay in school.
And the question mark button in the corner has the tour and help, any time you need them.
